questions.question: What is the difference between `os.Open`, `os.Create`, and `os.OpenFile`?
questions.title: os.Open, os.Create, and os.OpenFile
questions.direct_answer: `os.Open` opens an existing file read-only. `os.Create` opens a file for reading and writing, creates it when missing, and truncates existing content. `os.OpenFile` is the general form used when flags such as append, exclusive creation, or read-write access must be chosen explicitly. Every successful open returns a file that must be closed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `os.Open` uses read-only mode and does not create a missing file.
`os.Create` uses `O_RDWR | O_CREATE | O_TRUNC` and mode `0666` before the process umask.
`os.OpenFile` accepts explicit access and behaviour flags.
`O_TRUNC` destroys existing content; `O_APPEND` writes at the end.
Close every successfully opened `*os.File` and handle output errors.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`os.Open` is the narrow read-only helper. It is equivalent to calling `os.OpenFile(name, os.O_RDONLY, 0)`, so it fails when the file is missing and its result is meant for reads, seeks, or metadata operations.

`os.Create` is a stronger operation: it opens the file read-write, creates it when necessary, and truncates an existing file to zero length. That makes it suitable for replacing a report, but dangerous when old content must survive. The creation mode is `0666` before the operating system applies the process umask.

`os.OpenFile` exposes the decision directly. For example, a log writer commonly uses `os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREATE | os.O_APPEND` with a requested mode such as `0644`. An exclusive creator can add `O_EXCL` so an existing path causes an error instead of being overwritten.

All three return `*os.File` plus an error. I use the smallest helper whose contract matches the job, check the open error before touching the file, and close every successful handle. For output, write and close errors are part of correctness, not optional cleanup details.

sections.title: The helper name hides a specific OpenFile policy
sections.content:
The operating system needs an access mode and optional behaviours such as create, truncate, append, or exclusive creation. Go exposes that complete choice through `OpenFile`, then supplies `Open` and `Create` for two common combinations.

The flags describe what may happen to the file; the permission argument matters only when creation actually occurs. Choosing the wrong helper can therefore be destructive even when the following write code is correct.

sections.title: Concept guide · os.Open, os.Create, and os.OpenFile
sections.content:
`O_RDONLY`, `O_WRONLY`, and `O_RDWR` choose one access mode. Behaviour flags are combined with bitwise OR. `O_CREATE` permits creation, `O_TRUNC` clears an existing regular file when opened for writing, `O_APPEND` places each write at the end, and `O_EXCL` combined with `O_CREATE` rejects an existing path.

Opening succeeds before the returned handle can be used. If later work fails, the handle still owns an operating-system resource, which is why cleanup is arranged immediately after the nil-error check. A close failure on an output file must not be silently converted into success.

sections.title: The three opening contracts
sections.content:
| Call | Missing file | Existing content | Access | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `os.Open` | Error | Preserved | Read-only | Read or stream an existing file |
| `os.Create` | Created | Truncated | Read-write | Replace a file completely |
| `os.OpenFile` | Chosen by flags | Chosen by flags | Chosen by flags | Append, exclusive create, or custom access |

sections.title: Open, replace, and append to one temporary file
sections.content:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func check(err error) {
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
}

func main() {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "open-demo")
	check(err)
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	name := filepath.Join(dir, "notes.txt")
	check(os.WriteFile(name, []byte("old\n"), 0o600))

	input, err := os.Open(name)
	check(err)
	old, err := io.ReadAll(input)
	check(err)
	check(input.Close())
	fmt.Printf("before: %s", old)

	replacement, err := os.Create(name)
	check(err)
	_, err = io.WriteString(replacement, "fresh\n")
	check(err)
	check(replacement.Close())

	output, err := os.OpenFile(name, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_APPEND, 0)
	check(err)
	_, err = io.WriteString(output, "added\n")
	check(err)
	check(output.Close())

	final, err := os.ReadFile(name)
	check(err)
	fmt.Printf("after: %s", final)
}
```

questions.question: When should you use `os.ReadFile` or `os.WriteFile` instead of streaming?
questions.title: Whole-file helpers versus streaming
questions.direct_answer: Use `os.ReadFile` and `os.WriteFile` for small, bounded files when having the complete byte slice makes the code simpler. Stream through `*os.File`, `io.Reader`, `io.Writer`, Scanner, or Copy when data may be large, arrives gradually, or should be processed incrementally. Whole-file helpers use memory proportional to the content size.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Whole-file helpers are simple and return or accept one `[]byte`.
Their memory use grows with the entire file size.
Streaming keeps only a chunk or token in memory at a time.
Choose from a documented size bound, not from convenience alone.
`os.WriteFile` can leave partial output if a multi-step write fails.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`os.ReadFile` reads a named file completely and returns its bytes. `os.WriteFile` writes a complete byte slice, creating the file when absent or truncating it when present. They are excellent for bounded configuration, fixtures, and small generated files because ownership and error handling stay straightforward.

Their boundary is memory and latency. Reading a 20 MB file needs roughly that content in memory before processing can finish, while an unbounded upload or multi-gigabyte log can make whole-file loading unacceptable. Streaming exposes chunks or tokens so useful work can begin before the entire source is available.

For example, I might use `os.ReadFile` for a 4 KB template whose maximum size is controlled by the application. For an access log, I would open the file and scan lines, or copy it to another writer with `io.Copy`, keeping memory bounded independently of total size.

The decision is not that streaming is always better. It introduces lifecycle, partial-result, and token-boundary handling. I choose whole-file operations when the size limit is explicit and the complete value is genuinely needed; otherwise I preserve the stream and process it incrementally.

sections.title: The key distinction is when bytes become available
sections.content:
A whole-file API produces one completed value. That is convenient for parsing formats that require random access, but the caller cannot act until allocation and reading finish. A streaming API repeatedly transfers smaller pieces and can apply backpressure through the consumer.

Total file size and maximum record size are separate limits. A 10 GB newline file can be streamed with little memory, while one enormous line can still exceed a Scanner token limit. State the relevant bound explicitly.

sections.title: Concept guide · Whole-file helpers versus streaming
sections.content:
`ReadFile` opens, reads, and closes internally; a successful call returns a nil error rather than `io.EOF`. `WriteFile` performs multiple system operations, so a failure can leave a partially written destination. Applications requiring atomic replacement generally write a temporary file, sync as required, and rename under a carefully defined filesystem policy.

Streaming keeps resource ownership visible. The code must close files, handle each read or scan error, and decide what to do with output already produced when a later operation fails. That extra control is valuable only when size, latency, or pipeline composition needs it.

sections.title: Whole value or incremental stream
sections.content:
| Requirement | Whole-file helper | Streaming tool |
|---|---|---|
| Small bounded config | `os.ReadFile` | Usually unnecessary |
| Large log by line | Risks full-size allocation | `bufio.Scanner` or Reader |
| Copy a large body | Unnecessary intermediate slice | `io.Copy` |
| Need random access to all bytes | Natural fit | May need accumulation |
| Begin work before EOF | No | Yes |

questions.question: How do flags and file permissions work with `os.OpenFile`?
questions.title: OpenFile flags and creation permissions
questions.direct_answer: `os.OpenFile` combines one access mode with optional flags such as create, append, truncate, or exclusive creation. Its permission argument is used only if the call creates the file, and the process umask may remove requested bits. Reopening an existing file does not change its permissions; use `Chmod` when a mode change is intended.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Combine behaviour flags with bitwise OR.
`perm` matters only when `O_CREATE` creates a new file.
The process umask can remove requested permission bits.
Opening an existing file does not apply `perm` again.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `flag` argument has two jobs. One access flag selects read-only, write-only, or read-write access. Additional flags control behaviour: `O_CREATE` allows a missing file to be made, `O_APPEND` moves writes to the end, `O_TRUNC` clears existing content, and `O_EXCL` with create requires the path not to exist.

The `perm` value is a requested creation mode, not a permanent policy applied on every open. It is consulted only when this call creates the file, and the operating system applies the process umask before the final mode is stored. If the file already exists, passing `0600` does not repair broader permissions.

For example, `os.OpenFile(log, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND, 0640)` creates a missing log with requested owner/group access and appends future writes. If the log already exists as `0666`, this call leaves that mode alone; an explicit `Chmod` is a separate operation.

Flags also do not create parent directories, make a multi-write update atomic, or protect an untrusted path. I treat access, creation behaviour, permissions, and path safety as four separate decisions and handle every open, write, and close error.

sections.title: Flags choose behaviour; permissions describe new objects
sections.content:
A mode such as `0640` describes owner, group, and other permission bits requested for a newly created file. It does not override the process umask and does not rewrite metadata on an existing path.

This separation prevents an ordinary append from silently changing an administrator-managed file mode. It also means code that requires a particular existing mode must check and change it deliberately rather than relying on OpenFile's last argument.

sections.title: Concept guide · OpenFile flags and creation permissions
sections.content:
The destructive combinations deserve the most attention. `O_TRUNC` only makes sense with write access and discards prior content as part of opening. `O_APPEND` changes the placement of each write; seeking is not a replacement for append semantics when multiple writers may exist. `O_EXCL|O_CREATE` turns creation into a must-not-exist operation.

Permission literals are conventionally written in octal because each digit maps naturally to read, write, and execute bits. A file containing a secret may request `0600`, while an ordinary readable file may request `0644`, subject to deployment policy and umask.

sections.title: Common OpenFile choices
sections.content:
| Goal | Flags | If missing | If present |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read only | `O_RDONLY` | Error | Preserve |
| Replace | `O_WRONLY | O_CREATE | O_TRUNC` | Create with requested mode | Truncate, keep mode |
| Append | `O_WRONLY | O_CREATE | O_APPEND` | Create with requested mode | Preserve and append |
| Create only if new | `O_WRONLY | O_CREATE | O_EXCL` | Create | Error |

sections.title: Append without changing an existing file's mode
